128 THIRTY-SECOND REPORT U. S. CIVIL SERVICE COMMISSION, 
August 16, 1915. 
Miss Edna M. Ricketts, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a position in the classified service of the Government without reference to the civil-service rules. Miss Ricketts is the daughter of the late Thomas T. Ricketts, a veteran of Company C, Thirty-ninth Ohio Volunteer Infantry, who was an employee in the Government Printing Office from July, 1900, until the time of his death in April, 1913. She is an experienced stenographer and typewriter, and is the sole support of her widowed mother (now 74 years of age). : The Civil Service Commission does not recommend the issuance of an order in this case. 
August 19, 1915. 
First Sergeant William Feldman, United States Army, retired, may be admitted to 
examination for the classified service. Paragraph 1, civil-service Rule V, which provides that no person shall be admitted to examination unless he be a citizen of or owe allegiance to the United States, is hereby waived in his favor. Mr. Feldman is technically not a citizen of the United States, notwithstanding his service in the Army. In view of his honorable Army service of over 25 years, he being retired as first sergeant of Troop F, Sixth Cavalry, the commission concurs with the Secretary of War in recommending that Mr. Feldman be admitted to examination under waiver of the rule and with the understanding that he will without delay take the necessary steps to acquire citizenship. 
August 25, 1915. 
Mr. Robert W. F. Ogilve, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a position in the Naturalization Division of the Department of Labor without reference to the requirements of the civil-service rules. The commission was not advised of the reasons for the issuance of this order. 
August 25, 1915. 
Mr. C. Virgil Hinkle may be appointed to a competitive classified position in the postal service without reference to the civil-service rules. Mr. Hinkle was employed as a clerk in the Conway, Ark., post office from July 1, 1898, to June 28, 1913, when he was removed for insubordination, mistreatment of registered mail, and failure to comply with request of post-office inspectors to make good losses of registered mail for which, from circumstantial evidence, it was believed he wasresponsible. The assistant postmaster in office at the time of the embezzlement has confessed to rifling the mail in question. The Conway post office became classified on December 1, 1910, but Mr. Hinkle was not given a competitive classified status. 
This order is recommended by the Postmaster General, with the concurrence of the Civil Service Commission. 
August 26, 1915. 
The year limit upon eligibility for reinstatement is hereby waived to permit the reinstatement of Green A. Stephens in the postal service. 
Mr. Stephens was a carrier in the San Francisco post office from June 23, 1891, to April 12, 1905, when he was removed upon the charge of tampering with mail addressed 
to a patron in his district and using a race-track admission ticket contained in a letter so addressed. A careful reinvestigation by a post-office inspector resulted in the con￾clusion that beyond any reasonable doubt Mr. Stephens was not guilty of the charge for which he was removed from the postal service. The Postmaster General states that there is no question in his mind but that a distinct injustice was done in separating Carrier Stephens from the service on the flimsy and prejudiced evidence which was adduced in the case. He therefore recommends that an Executive order be issued to reinstate him in the service, and the Civil Service Commission, after careful review of the case, concurs in this recommendation. 
September 2, 1915. 
Miss Bertha Goldberg, of Washington, D. C., may be appointed to a clerkship in the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce, Department of Commerce, without 
reference to the civil-service rules. . Miss Goldberg has passed the stenographer and typewriter examination with an average of 84.29, and has been serving temporarily in the bureau since February 25, 1915. The chief of the Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce and the Acting Secretary of Commerce recommend her permanent appointment on account of her unusual ability and efficiency as a stenographer and typewriter and the exceptional

September 8, 1915. 
Mr. Clifford B. Potter may be reinstated in the postal service without reference to the length of his separation from the service. Mr. Potter was appointed a substitute carrier in the Jersey City, N. Brockenshire, chief musician, United States Army, retired, may be appointed as inspector of musical instruments at $780 per annum, Quartermaster Corps of the Army, without examination under the civil-service rules.
